newsitem.title: MEXICO: FOCUS - Mexico helps Serfin before sale.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Mexico helps Serfin before sale.

text.p: Mexico's third largest bank, Serfin, unveiled spectacular losses on Tuesday prior to its sale to a foreign partner and shocked analysts by selling a major chunk of stock to the government.

For months analysts have waited for news of the sale of 19.9 percent of Grupo Financiero Serfin to a unit of London-based HSBC Holdings Plc. They had hoped it would be announced to coincide with the 1996 results.

On Tuesday, the results of its Banca Serfin banking unit came out showing a massive 7.446 billion peso loss in the 12-month period, versus a 22 million peso profit in 1995 -- the legacy of a major reserve-building effort.

But there was no hard news of a sale. The only suggestion that a deal was nearing came from Serfin chairman Adrian Sada, who told reporters in the northern industrial city of Monterrey he expected news in 48 hours.

Instead, Serfin announced the sale of 10.3 billion pesos of mortgage loans to the government's bank insurance fund, Fobaproa, the third major loan sale to be announced since the government prematurely declared bailouts over last December.

In exchange, Serfin paid in cash two billion pesos of reserves to Fobaproa, charging the same amount to capital. To offset that charge, Fobaproa bought two billion pesos of Serfin common stock, plus "contingent right of reinbursement" for losses on the loans of up to 3.665 billion that could shrink.
That, said Susana Hornelos of Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, will mean "a lot more dilution" and could have negative consequences for the stock price.

"People haven't done their homework," she said. "You're going to have dilution from HSBC and dilution from Fobaproa, plus a drain on future earnings for repayment to Fobaproa from the contingent right of reinbursement."

She also noted that even after the mortgage loan sell-off, Serfin's past-due loan ratio under new U.S. GAAP accounting standards as a percentage of total loans was 22.6 percent, worse than rivals Banamex and Bancomer.

Serfin's lingering problems -- and its need for additional government support -- were no surprise to analysts. They say since the economic crisis erupted in 1994, the bank's owners have been forced to sink more than double what they paid for it into recapitalizing the stricken bank.

Prior to the crisis, Serfin was already suffering from a shortage of cheap funding from deposits, and the cost of borrowing in the money markets became a crippling burden when interest rates sky-rocketed in 1995.

Laura Berdeja, Latin American bank analyst at Santander Investments, said the government's decision to become a shareholder showed it was "prepared to go the extra mile" for Serfin prior to the sale to a foreign partner, and she said it was possible the move could be a good deal for the government.

But she also noted that the government deal presented "stock overhang" that may worry investors. She estimated dilution from the sale to Fobaproa and the future partner would be about 44 percent, in addition to the 52 percent already stemming from its past recapitalization efforts.
For its potential partner, she said Serfin's efforts to reserve heavily against bad loans showed it was concentrating on restructuring the bank to strengthen its balance sheet.
The new partner, she said, "would be acquiring a much cleaner shell to promote business later."
But when it does start actively going back to banking again, competition will be stiff. "It may have a harder time catching up," she said.
